title: Homily II — Not a goddess but the Mother of God

edition.locus: Migne, PG 96 (Paris, 1860), Homily II on the Dormition, cols. 741-744 (PDF leaves 412-413)

source_text: Δεῦτε τοιγαροῦν, καὶ ἡμεῖς σήμερον ἑορτὴν ἐξόδιον τῇ Μητρὶ τοῦ Θεοῦ ἑορτάσωμεν, οὐκ αὐλούς τινας καὶ κορύβαντας φέροντες, καὶ τὰ τῆς μητρὸς τῶν ψευδωνύμων θεῶν, ὡς αὐτοὶ λέγουσι, θιασεύοντες ὄργια, ἣν πολύτεκνον μυθοπλαστοῦσιν οἱ ἄφρονες, ὁ δὲ τῆς ἀληθείας λόγος παρίστησιν ἄτεκνον. Οἷα δαίμονες ταῦτα καὶ σκιώδη φαντάσματα, ὃ μὴ πεφύκασιν εἰκαίως ὑποκρινόμενοι, τῶν πλανωμένων τὴν ἄνοιαν ἐσχηκότες ἐπίκουρον. Γεννᾷ γὰρ πῶς ἐκ συνδυασμοῦ τὸ ἀσώματον; καὶ τίνα τρόπον μιχθήσεται; καὶ πῶς Θεὸς τὸ μὴ ὂν μὲν πρότερον, πρὸς δὲ γένεσιν παραγόμενον; Ὅτι γὰρ ἀσώματον τὸ δαιμόνιον φῦλον, παντί που δῆλον, καὶ αὐτοῖς τοῖς τὰ νοητὰ τυφλώττουσιν ὄμματα. Ἔφη γάρ που τῶν ἑαυτοῦ λόγων ὁ Ὅμηρος, τῶν ἀξίων αὐτοῦ θεῶν ὑφηγούμενος τὴν κατάστασιν· Οὐ πυρὸν ἐσθίουσιν, οὐ πίνουσιν αἴθοπα οἶνον, Τοὔνεκ' ἀναίμονές εἰσι, καὶ ἀθάνατοι καλέονται. Οὐ σῖτον ἐσθίουσι, φησὶν, οὐ τὸν θερμαντικὸν οἶνον πίνουσι. Τούτου χάριν ἀναίμονές εἰσι, τουτέστιν αἷμα οὐκ ἔχουσι, καὶ ἀθάνατοι ὀνομάζονται. Καιρίως ὡς ἀληθῶς ἔφη τὸ, καλέονται. Ἀθάνατοι γὰρ καλοῦνται· οὐκ εἰσὶ δὲ τοῦθ' ὅπερ καλοῦνται· τὸν γὰρ τῆς κακίας τεθνήκασι θάνατον. Ἡμεῖς δὲ οἷς Θεός ἐστι τὸ λατρευόμενον, Θεὸς οὐκ ἐκ μὴ ὄντος εἰς τὸ εἶναι παραγενόμενος, ἀλλ' ἀεὶ ὢν ἐκ τοῦ ἀεὶ ὄντος ὑπὲρ αἰτίαν, καὶ λόγον, καὶ ἔννοιαν καὶ χρόνου, καὶ φύσεως, Μητέρα Θεοῦ τιμῶμεν καὶ σέβομεν, οὐ τῆς αὐτοῦ θεότητος ἐξ αὐτῆς τὴν ἄχρονον ὑπογράφοντες γέννησιν· ἡ γὰρ τοῦ Θεοῦ Λόγου γέννησις ἄχρονός τε καὶ τῷ Πατρὶ συναΐδιος· δευτέραν δὲ καθομολογοῦμεν γέννησιν, καθ' ἑκούσιον σάρκωσιν, τὴν ταύτης αἰτίαν, καὶ εἰδότες, καὶ φάσκοντες. Σαρκοῦται γὰρ ὁ ὢν ἀνάρχως ἀσώματος, δι' ἡμᾶς, καὶ διὰ τὴν ἡμετέραν σωτηρίαν, ἵνα τῷ ὁμοίῳ τὸν ὅμοιον διασώσηται· καὶ σαρκούμενος ἐκ ταύτης τῆς ἱερᾶς Παρθένου ἀσυνδυάστως τίκτεται, αὐτὸς μένων ὅλος Θεὸς, καὶ ὅλος γινόμενος ἄνθρωπος, αὐτὸς ὅλος Θεὸς μετὰ τῆς σαρκὸς αὐτοῦ, καὶ ὅλος ἄνθρωπος μετὰ τῆς αὐτοῦ ὑπερθέου θεότητος. Οὕτω Θεοῦ Μητέρα τὴν Παρθένον ταύτην γινώσκοντες, τὴν ταύτης πανηγυρίζομεν κοίμησιν, οὐ Θεὸν ταύτην φημίζοντες· ἄπαγε, τῆς Ἑλληνικῆς τερθρείας τὰ τοιαῦτα μυθεύματα· ἐπεὶ καὶ θάνατον αὐτῆς καταγγέλλομεν· ἀλλὰ σαρκωθέντος Θεοῦ Μητέρα γινώσκοντες.
pass_a_gloss: Come (δεῦτε) therefore, let us also today celebrate (ἑορτάζω) a departure/funeral feast for the Mother of God, not carrying (φέρω) some flutes (αὐλοί) and Corybants, and celebrating in revel-bands (θιασεύω) the orgies/rites (ὄργια) of the mother (μήτηρ) of the falsely-named gods (θεοί), as they themselves say, whom the senseless (ἄφρονες) fable-fashion as many-childed, but the word (λόγος) of truth (ἀλήθεια) presents as childless (ἄτεκνος). Such [are] demons these and shadowy (σκιώδη) phantoms, what they are not by nature (πέφυκα) randomly/vainly (εἰκαίως) acting the part, having had the folly (ἄνοια) of the deceived as helper. For how does the bodiless beget (γεννάω) from coupling? and in what manner will it be mixed (μίγνυμι)? and how [is] God what was not before, but is brought (παράγω) to coming-to-be (γένεσις)? For that the demonic race (φῦλον) [is] bodiless, [is] plain (δῆλον) to everyone, even to those blind in the intelligible (νοητά) eyes (ὄμματα). For Homer (Ὅμηρος) said somewhere in his own words, setting forth the condition of gods worthy (ἄξιοι) of him: They eat not wheat (πυρός), they drink not fiery/sparkling (αἴθοψ) wine (οἶνος); therefore (τοὔνεκα) bloodless they are, and are called immortals (ἀθάνατοι). They do not eat grain (σῖτος), he says, they do not drink the warming wine. For this reason they are bloodless, that is, have no blood (αἷμα), and are named (ὀνομάζω) immortal. Aptly (καιρίως) truly he said the 'are called'. For they are called immortals; but are not what they are called; for they have died (θνῄσκω) the death of wickedness (κακία). But we, for whom what is worshipped (λατρεύω) is God, God not from non-being (μὴ ὄν) come into being (τὸ εἶναι), but always being (ἀεὶ ὤν) from the always-being, above cause (αἰτία) and reason/word (λόγος) and thought (ἔννοια) and time (χρόνος) and nature (φύσις), honour (τιμάω) and revere (σέβω) [the] Mother of God, not delineating (ὑπογράφω) from her the timeless (ἄχρονος) generation (γέννησις) of his Godhead (θεότης); for the generation of God the Word [is] timeless and co-eternal with the Father; but a second (δευτέρα) generation we confess, according to voluntary (ἑκούσιος) incarnation (σάρκωσις), both knowing (οἶδα) and asserting (φάσκω) the cause of this. For he who is without beginning (ἀνάρχως) bodiless is made flesh (σαρκόω) for us, and for our salvation (σωτηρία), so that by the like (ὅμοιον) he may save (διασῴζω) the like; and being made flesh from this holy Virgin (Παρθένος) he is born (τίκτω) without coupling, himself remaining (μένω) whole (ὅλος) God and becoming whole man (ἄνθρωπος), himself whole God with his flesh (σάρξ), and whole man with his super-divine (ὑπέρθεος) Godhead. Thus knowing (γινώσκω) this Virgin [as] Mother of God, we celebrate in festival her falling-asleep (κοίμησις), not proclaiming (φημίζω) her God/goddess (Θεόν); away (ἄπαγε) [with] such fables of Hellenic (Ἑλληνική) quackery (τερθρεία); since we also announce her death; but knowing [her as] Mother of God made flesh.
pass_b_english: Come then, let us too keep today a feast of departure for the Mother of God. We do not bring flutes and Corybants, nor do we celebrate the rites of the mother of the falsely named gods, as they themselves call her, whom fools make out in their myths to be the mother of many children, but whom the word of truth shows to be childless. These are demons and shadowy phantoms, idly playing the part of what they are not by nature, who have found an ally in the folly of those who are led astray. For how does what is bodiless beget by coupling? In what way will it mingle? And how is that a god which did not exist before but is brought into being? For it is surely plain to everyone, even to those who are blind in the eyes of the mind, that the race of demons is bodiless.

For Homer said somewhere in his poems, describing the condition of the gods worthy of him: "They eat no wheat, they drink no gleaming wine; therefore they are bloodless, and are called immortals." They do not eat grain, he says, they do not drink wine that warms; for this reason they are bloodless, that is, they have no blood, and are named immortal. He was truly apt in saying "are called". For they are called immortal, but they are not what they are called: they have died the death of wickedness.

But we, for whom the one we worship is God, God who did not come into being out of what was not, but who always is, from him who always is, beyond cause and reason and thought, beyond time and nature, honour and revere the Mother of God. We do not ascribe to her the timeless birth of his Godhead, for the birth of God the Word is timeless and co-eternal with the Father; but we confess a second birth, by his voluntary incarnation, and we both know and declare its cause. For he who is without beginning and bodiless becomes flesh for us and for our salvation, so that he might save like by like; and becoming flesh from this holy Virgin, he is born without coupling, himself remaining wholly God and becoming wholly man, the same wholly God with his flesh and wholly man with his transcendent Godhead. So, knowing this Virgin to be Mother of God, we celebrate her falling asleep, not proclaiming her a goddess (away with such fables, the trickery of the pagans!), since we also proclaim her death, but knowing her to be the Mother of God made flesh.

choices.note: No Scripture is quoted or clearly alluded to; the print gives no margin reference.
The verse is Homer, Iliad 5.341-342 (edition note 55), quoted loosely: the print has πυρὸν ἐσθίουσιν ("eat wheat") where Homer's text has σῖτον; the homilist's paraphrase then uses σῖτον.
The verse is kept inline as the print sets it, in quotation marks.

The "mother of the falsely named gods" with her flutes and Corybants is the Phrygian Mother of the Gods (Cybele, identified with Rhea); she is not named in the Greek, so the name is not added to the text.
"Childless" means that, since the pagan gods do not exist, she has no real children.
"For us and for our salvation" (δι' ἡμᾶς καὶ διὰ τὴν ἡμετέραν σωτηρίαν) is the wording of the Nicene Creed, not Scripture.
τὴν ταύτης αἰτίαν ("its cause") is taken as the cause of the second birth, which the next sentence gives with γάρ; it could also be read "[knowing and declaring her] its cause".
λατρευόμενον rendered "the one we worship" (λατρεία, the worship due to God), while the Mother of God is honoured and revered (τιμῶμεν καὶ σέβομεν): the distinction is the author's and is kept.
Θεὸν ταύτην φημίζοντες rendered "proclaiming her a goddess" (θεός can be feminine), which the pagan contrast requires.
Ἑλληνικὴ τερθρεία ("Hellenic quackery") rendered "the trickery of the pagans", since "Hellene" here means pagan.
ἑορτὴ ἐξόδιος rendered "a feast of departure".
The irony of "gods worthy of him" is the author's.
Οἷα δαίμονες ταῦτα: the subject is the false gods just named (PG Latin "Daemones enim ista sunt"), so it is rendered "These are demons", not a general remark about demons.
Review confirmed the printed Homeric line (Οὐ πυρὸν ἐσθίουσιν) and τὴν ταύτης αἰτίαν on the page images (leaves 412-413); the PG Latin "cujus causam et novimus" supports "its cause".
